text:
Not everyone agrees. The evidence is mixed: a 2024 *Nature* RCT (Bloom et al., Trip.com) found hybrid work had no effect on productivity or promotions and cut attrition by about a third. A memo claiming consensus will be easy to rebut. The claim you can defend is narrower: fully remote work can hurt some kinds of output, especially collaborative work and work by junior staff.

Three bullets that hold up (verify figures against the sources before sending):

- **Output on some tasks fell under fully remote work.** Atkin, Schoar & Shinde (2023) found roughly 18% lower productivity among fully remote data-entry workers in India. Gibbs, Mengel & Siemroth (2021) found lower output per hour at an Asian IT firm, with hours worked rising substantially.
- **Collaboration networks become more siloed.** Yang et al. (2022, *Nature Human Behaviour*), using Microsoft data, found remote work reduced cross-team ties and shifted communication toward asynchronous channels, which hurts information flow and innovation.
- **Junior employees get less mentoring and feedback.** Emanuel, Harrington & Pallais (2023) found software engineers received less feedback from senior colleagues when they were remote, which can slow skill development and long-run output.

Strongest counterargument: these studies mostly cover fully remote setups and specific roles, while the best hybrid RCT shows no productivity loss. If your policy question is about hybrid, these bullets don't support it. If it's about fully remote or junior-heavy teams, they do.
